front: Farming
back: (pg. 2) A form of marketing where a licensee specializes in a particular neighborhood or type of property to increase their chances of success.

front: Going Concern Value
back: The Appraisal Concept of Value of a profitable business enterprise or opportunities. Because the business is profitable it is expected to continue (Includes Income, Tangible and intangible Assets, Goodwill (reputation) plus and real estate property)-Also see Chapter 17 for more details.

front: Broker Associate
back: (pg. 17) A licensee with a broker’s license (who has passed the brokers exam and is now licensed as broker) but continues to work/act and be employed under the direction of an actively licensed real estate broker.

front: Broker License Requirements
back: To be eligible for a broker’s license a sales associate must be active for 24 months in the past 5 years and successfully complete the 72-hour pre-licensing education and pass the class exam, with a 70% and the state exam with 75%. (page 17)

front: DBPR process for licensing denial
back: DBPR has 30 days to review for errors and omissions and must be either approved or denied within 90 days from application date. Notify applicant in writing of the reason for denial and advise the applicant regarding the right to request a formal hearing. (pg. 21-22)

front: If the application is denied by DBPR
back: The applicant will be notified in writing of the reason for the denial and advised of the right to request a formal hearing within 21 before an administrative law judge. (pg. 21)

front: A sales or broker associate may work only for _____ at a time. Working for a broker and an owner-developer constitutes a violation of F.S. 475 unless the owner developer pays the licensee on a_____. (pg. 25)
back:
A sales or broker associate may work only for one broker at a time. Working for a 
broker and an owner-developer constitutes a violation of F.S. 475 unless the 
owner developer pays the licensee on a salary basis only, no commission, no 
bonus. (pg. 25)

front: Registration Requirements for owner Developer
back: Owner developers are registered but NOT licensed; Brokers are licensed and registered. Pg 25

front: People who are exempt from license
back: Attorney in fact (person with a POA authority); Attorney’s and CPA when acting in the scope of their profession.

front: Attorney in fact
back: (pg. 28) A person given authority by power of attorney to represent or act on behalf of another.

front: First renewal requirement
back: (pg. 26, 41) Licensee must successfully complete the 45-hr. post licensing class, pass the test with a 75% to qualify for the license renewal. Failure to complete the Post Licensing education Will result in a null and voided license. License renewals fall on Sept 30 and March 31st every 2 years.

front: Injunction
back: (pg. 37) a Court Order (Issued only by the Court) The Department may SEEK an injunction but may not Issue an injunction.

front: What is a Cease and Desist Order, and when would FREC issue one?
back: A Cease and Desist Order directs an unlicensed individual acting as a sales associate without a valid real estate license to STOP the unauthorized activity.

front: What actions may FREC take against an unlicensed individual, and what action can FREC NOT issue?
back:
FREC may issue:

1. Administrative fine
2. Citation
3. Cease-and-desist order

FREC may seek an injunction through the circuit court, but FREC itself never issues an injunction.

front: Who may exercise the Executive Powers of DBPR?
back: The chairperson of FREC, acting alone. (pg. 38)

front: The maximum fine amount that the FREC (Commission) may impose is ______ per violation. (pg. 37)
Disciplinary action of the commission (FREC):
back:
(pg. 37) 
• Fine of $500 up to $5000 per offense, 
• Reprimand (Warning-1st offense), 
• Probation for up to 90 days, 
• Suspension for up to 10 years, or 
• Permanent Revocation.

front: A licensed that is relinquished to the DBPR is said to be _______.
back: Cancelled.

front: An agent authorized to perform a single act on behalf of the principal.
back: (pg. 51) Special Agent

front: A ___________ is an individual who employs a broker to represent them in a fiduciary agency relationship (single agency).
back: Principal

front: A relationship of trust and confidence between the agent/broker and the principal (employer). Both the agent and broker are bound by fiduciary duties when acting as single agents.
back: Fiduciary Duties

front: When do both the broker and associate owe fiduciary duties to the principal/client?
back: When the broker gives the associate permission to work directly with the principal/client, both the broker and associate owe fiduciary duties to the principal/client.

front: Do brokers and agents have to present all offers?
back:
Yes. They must present ALL offers, including oral offers, unless the seller says otherwise or the listing contract gives different instructions.

Not presenting an offer = violation of FS 475. (pg. 55)

front:
Can only represent buyer or seller but not in the same transaction. 
Dual representation is a violation of Florida Statute 475.  Both associates and 
broker owe fiduciary duties to the principal(client). (pg. 55)
back: Single agent

front: Who can a Single Agent represent?
back:
A single agent can represent ONLY the buyer OR the seller, not both in the same transaction.

Dual representation = violation of FS 475
Broker and associate owe fiduciary duties to the principal. (pg. 55)

front: Requirement for an office
back: (Pg 68) The office must consist of at least one room where negotiations are conducted in privacy, and where books and records are kept. It must be of stationary construction. Motor/Mobile home does not qualify as an office.

front: Is the main office registration transferable when the office moves?
back: Yes. The main office registration is transferable. (pg. 68)

front: What happens to a branch office registration when the branch moves?
back: A branch office requires a new registration when it moves. (pg. 68)

front: Can a branch office be closed and reopened at the same location during the same license period?
back: Yes. A reissue can be requested as long as the registration is still valid. (pg. 68)

front: Postdated checks are considered to be ______ and can be accepted as ______ with the seller's approval.
back: Postdated checks are considered to be promissory notes and can be accepted as earnest money with the seller's approval. (P. 71-1)

front: The Sales or Broker Associate must give the check to the broker no later than _____.
back: No later than the end of the next business day.

front: When must the broker deposit the post-dated check?
back: Within or before the end of the 3rd business day.

front: List the approved depositories for earnest money deposits.
back: Title Companies, Savings & Loans, Credit Unions. They must be located and doing business in Florida. Not an interest-bearing account held in a stock or bond brokerage house.

front: Procedure for good faith doubt, or a disputed deposit of escrowed funds.
back: The broker must give written notice to the Commission within 15 business days from the date of the last pary's demand. The broker is then required to institute a dispute resolution procedure within 30 days.

front: If a seller refuses an offer that meets the listing agreement, who owes the broker the commission?
back: The seller owes the broker the commission because the broker fulfilled the employment agreement and earned the commission.

front: Who can a sales associate sue if their employing broker fails to pay an agreed commission?
back: Only the broker who failed to pay the commission—even if the sales associate has resigned and started working for a different broker. (pg. 79)

front: When can a licensee receive a referral commission?
back: A licensee can receive a referral commission for referring a buyer or seller, as long as they do not participate in the sale. (pg. 78)

front: Can a Florida broker pay a referral fee to an out-of-state real estate broker?
back: Yes, as long as the referring broker does not participate in the transaction. (pg. 78)

front: What is required for a real estate brokerage partnership?
back: At least one partner must have an active broker’s license.

front: Can an inactive broker or unlicensed person be a partner in a real estate brokerage partnership?
back: Yes, but they cannot perform real estate services and must register with the Department.

front: Can a sales associate or broker associate be a partner in a real estate brokerage partnership?
back: No. Any partner who provides real estate services to the public must have an active broker’s license.

front:
A type of business relationship that has been formed by two or 
more people who agree to combine efforts for a single business transaction. 
(Pg 82)
back: Joint Venture

front: What must a for-profit corporation's name include?
back: The name must include “Company,” “Incorporated,” or an abbreviation such as Corp., Inc., or Co. (pg. 83) **A business must be legally incorporated to use “Company” in its name.**

front: What is required for a Brokerage Corporation?
back: It must be registered and have at least one officer who is a licensed broker. (pg. 83)

front: Can a Limited Partnership perform real estate brokerage services?
back: Yes. A Limited Partnership may register with the Department to perform brokerage services. (pg. 81)

front:
Acting in an excessively negligent manner. (pg. 98) E.g. 
Failing to collect an escrow deposit as due in the contract.
back: Culpable negligence

front:
A property that has defective title and may be didicult to convey. The proper course of action if a listed property 
is found to be not merchantable is: the Broker must notify the seller 
immediately regarding the condition of title. (pg. 99)
back: Properties with Liens

front: When must a broker inform a buyer about a mortgage or lien on a property?
back: The broker must inform the prospective buyer before the buyer pays any part of the sales price.

front: Is it legal for a broker to sell a property knowing the title is unmerchantable?
back: No. It is fraudulent and dishonest dealing for a broker to offer the property for sale knowing the title is unmerchantable.

front: What must the Department do if a license application is denied?
back:
The Department must:

Notify the applicant in writing
Give the reason for the denial
Inform the applicant they can request a formal hearing within 21 days to protest the denial.

front:
Applicable to Sellers. The illegal practice of inducing 
homeowners to list and sell their properties by telling them minorities are 
moving into their neighborhoods and as a consequence will lose 
value/equity. (pg. 116)
back: Blockbusting

front: What does the ADA require for properties built before 1990?
back: Landlords must make necessary modifications to comply with ADA when readily achievable and economically feasible — not regardless of cost. (pg. 119)

front: What must properties built after 1990 do?
back: They must comply with ADA building codes. (pg. 119)

front: When the landlord commingles security deposits with their own funds, a ______ is required to protect the escrowed funds from loss. (pg. 122)
back: Surety Bond

front: An estate involving ownership.
back: Freehold Estate

front: What is Real Property?
back: Real property includes the land, improvements, and the ownership rights and interests associated with them. (pg. 130)

front:
Water rights a property owner has on a property that 
borders a river or stream (Moving Waters).
back: Riparian Rights. (p.131)

front:
The opposite of erosion. The gradual accumulation/addition in soil 
or growth of land due to natural causes.
back: Accretion  (pg. 131)

front:
When form of estate has ownership vested to one owner/Sole-ownership/No co-
ownership?
back: Estate in Severalty (p.133)

front: What type of ownership has equal rights of use and possession and the right of inheritability?
back: Tenancy in Common. (p. 134) **Owners may acquire their interests through the same or different deeds.

front: What type of ownership has the Right of Survivorship?
back:
Joint Tenancy (Joint Estate). Two or more people receive equal, undivided interests at the same time, in the same deed, with equal PITT:
Possession, Interest, Time, Title. (pg. 134)

Tip: Joint Tenancy = Right of Survivorship.

front: What type of ownership is only between husband and wife and includes the right of survivorship?
back:
Tenancy by the Entireties. If they divorce, the title becomes Tenancy in Common unless the court orders otherwise. (pgs. 134–135)

Tip: Entireties = married couple + survivorship.

front: What is a Tenancy for Years?
back:
A leasehold estate for a specific period of time with a definite beginning and ending date. (pg. 136)

Tip: Tenancy for Years = definite start + definite end.

front: What is Eminent Domain?
back:
The government’s right to take private property for public use with fair compensation.

Key Rule: The owner may protest the amount of compensation, but cannot refuse the taking.

Example: A city takes private land to build a school. (Shopping Center-Movie Theater is private property, not for public use/ *****NOT 
ELIGIBLE FOR EMINENT DOMAIN PROCEEDINGS**** 
Eligible properties: School, VA Hospital, Railroad, Power plant- Public property. (pg. 
143, 153)

front: What is required to transfer title by deed?
back: The grantor’s signature and 2 witnesses.

front: Who must sign a deed for it to be valid?
back: Only the GRANTOR must sign the deed. The GRANTEE does NOT need to sign.

front: What is a Quitclaim Deed used for?
back:
A deed with NO warranties that is mainly used to correct title defects or clear clouds on title.

Common uses include:

Divorce — one spouse gives up their interest to the other.
Removing easements.

Tip: It is “Quitclaim,” NOT “Quick Claim.” (pg. 150)

front: What should brokers advise parties to do with documents that could affect title?
back: Advise them to record the documents immediately. (p.152)

front: What is a Gross Lease?
back:
A lease where the tenant pays a fixed rent, while the landlord pays all expenses, including taxes, insurance, and maintenance.

Tip: Gross Lease = Tenant pays rent; landlord pays expenses. (pg. 155)

front: Which specific liens are Superior and which are Junior?
back:
Superior: Property taxes, special assessments
Junior: Mortgage, construction lien
(pgs. 157–158)

front: What is the primary reference point in a metes and bounds legal description?
back: The Point of Beginning (POB). (pg. 164)

front: How many sections are in a township?
back: A township is divided into 36 sections.

front: How large is a township, and how many acres are in a section?
back:
Township: 6 miles × 6 miles = 36 square miles
Section: 640 acres

front: One acre contains how many square feet?
One township section contains how many acres?
What is an Assessor Parcel Number (APN)?
back:
A unique parcel number assigned by the county property assessor to identify each individual property.

Tip: Every county has its own system.
Example: Miami = Folio #; Broward = Property ID. (pg. 173)

front: What is the transfer of contractual rights and responsibilities from one person to another called?
back:
Assignment.

Key Rule: The seller is NOT released from the contract unless released in writing. (pg. 183)

front: What type of contract has terms and conditions that are inferred from the parties’ actions or conduct?
back:
Implied Contract.

Example: Hiring a painter implies they will use exterior-grade paint on the outside of a home. (pg. 184)

front: What is a contract that cannot be enforced or performed under the law called?
back: A Void Contract — it is no longer valid and unenforceable. (pg. 185)

front: What is a Suit for Specific Performance?
back:
A lawsuit that asks the court to order a party to fulfill their contract obligations.

Example: If a seller fails to close, the buyer may sue for Specific Performance, and the court may order the seller to complete the sale. (pg. 188)

front: What is a lawsuit where the injured party asks the court for financial compensation for harm suffered called?
back:
Suit for Damages — the injured party sues to receive money for the harm suffered.

Key Rule: Recovery Fund = relief, not a remedy.

front: What are damages that are defined and agreed upon in the contract ahead of time called?
back: Liquidated Damages — damages specified in the contract, such as a seller keeping the buyer’s escrow deposit when the buyer defaults.

front: What must sellers of residential property in Florida disclose?
back: Material Defects — any fact that could have a significant and reasonable impact on the property’s value.

front: Does an “as-is” provision relieve the seller from disclosing material defects?
back: No. An “as-is” provision does NOT relieve the seller of the responsibility to disclose material defects.

front: What type of listing agreement provides the best protection for the broker to receive a commission, regardless of who sells the property?
back:
Exclusive Right of Sale Listing — the broker is entitled to the commission as long as all contingencies are fulfilled, regardless of who is the procuring cause of the sale. (Pg. 197)

Example: The seller agrees to pay the broker a commission even if someone else actually sells the property.

front: What type of state allows the buyer (mortgagor) to hold legal title to the property while the mortgage serves as a lien?
back: Lien Theory State — the seller delivers the deed at closing, and the buyer becomes the legal owner on the day of closing. Florida is a lien theory state. (pgs. 208–209)

front: What legal document specifies the mortgage loan amount, interest rate, loan term, and repayment schedule?
back: Promissory Note — evidence of the debt and the borrower’s promise to repay the loan. (pg. 208)

front: What document is sent by the lender after a mortgage loan is fully repaid and must be recorded to remove the mortgage lien?
back: Letter of Satisfaction (Satisfaction of Mortgage) — the lender sends it to the mortgagor within 60 days of final payment, and it must be recorded in the public records to release the mortgage lien. (pg. 209)

front: What mortgage clause limits the lender’s right to collect beyond the foreclosure sale proceeds and prevents a deficiency judgment?
back: Exculpatory Clause — limits the lender’s recovery to the amount received from the foreclosure sale proceeds. (pg. 211)

front: What is another name for a land contract, installment sales contract, agreement for deed, or conditional sales contract?
back: Contract for Deed (p.217)

front: What is the mortgagor’s right to redeem their interest in a mortgaged property by paying the amount owed before the foreclosure sale?
back: Equity of Redemption — the right to pay the lender the amount owed and redeem the property before the foreclosure sale. (pg. 218)

front: Who receives any surplus funds remaining after all lien holders are paid from a foreclosure sale?
back: The Mortgagor — any remaining surplus funds are paid to the mortgagor (property owner).

front: What does the FHA do instead of making mortgage loans?
back: The FHA insures loans made by approved local lenders. It does not make or originate the loans. (p.228)

front: What are the FHA qualifying ratios for housing and total obligations?
back:
31% Housing / 43% Total Obligations (pg. 229)

Memory Tip: 31 / 43 = FHA

front: What type of loans are guaranteed by the VA and originated by VA-approved lenders?
back: VA Loans — guaranteed by the Veterans Administration and originated by VA-approved lenders. They are only for owner-occupied properties. (pg. 231)

front: What is GNMA (Ginnie Mae), and what role does it play in the mortgage market?
back: GNMA (Ginnie Mae) operates in the secondary mortgage market and guarantees mortgage-backed securities. It does not make or originate mortgage loans.

front: What is Ginnie Mae (GNMA) primarily engaged in, and what does it provide?
back: Ginnie Mae (GNMA) provides a secondary market for FHA and VA loans and guarantees payment on securities backed by residential mortgages.

front: What protected categories must lenders ignore when qualifying loan applicants under ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act)?
back:
A-R-R-S-M-N

A = Age
R = Race
R = Religion
S = Sex
M = Marital status
N = Nationality

Memory Tip: “A Real Realtor Sells Many Neighborhoods” → A-R-R-S-M-N (pg. 248)

front: What does TILA require a lender to do when the terms or costs of financing change?
back:
Truth in Lending Act (TILA) requires the lender to re-disclose the Loan Estimate (LE) when there is a change in the interest rate, loan amount, number of payments, or applicable costs. (pg. 249)

Memory Tip: TILA = Tell It Again when loan terms or costs change.

front: What triggers TILA disclosure requirements in a real estate advertisement?
back:
Using ANY NUMBER in the advertisement triggers TILA disclosure requirements.

Examples:

“Interest rate as low as 4%”
“Only $10,000 down”
“Payments as low as $1,200”

Key Rule: Assumable Mortgage is NOT a triggering term because it contains no number. (pg. 249)

Memory Tip: TILA = Any Number → Trigger!

front: How is a binder deposit shown on the Closing Disclosure?
back:
A Binder Deposit is shown as a CREDIT to the Buyer. Even though the buyer paid the deposit, it is not a debit because it is credited toward the purchase price. (pg. 266)

Memory Tip: Binder Deposit = Buyer Credit.

front: When is monthly mortgage interest typically paid?
back:
Mortgage interest is typically paid in arrears, meaning after the interest has accrued.

Memory Tip: Arrears = After

front: If a buyer assumes the seller’s loan, who has paid the interest for the month of the sale?
back:
The seller has paid no interest for that month, so the interest is prorated at closing.

Memory Tip: Sale = Split the Interest

front: How are documentary stamps on a deed calculated in Florida?
back:
$0.70 for every $100 (or fraction of $100) of the sales price.
If there is any amount left over after dividing by $100, charge another $0.70.

Example:

$200,000 → $1,400
$200,050 → $1,400.70
$200,100 → $1,400.70

Miami-Dade: $0.60 per $100 (or fraction thereof). (pg. 266)

Memory Tip: Any leftover = another stamp.

front: When is the Florida State Intangible Tax on mortgages paid?
back:
The State Intangible Tax is paid on new mortgages only.

Memory Tip: New Mortgage = Intangible Tax

front: What concept of value applies to a profitable business that is expected to continue operating?
back:
Going Concern — the value of a profitable business that is expected to continue operating. (pg. 295; Ch. 17 pg. 333)

Memory Tip: Going Concern = Business keeps going.

front: What is the value of a failing business that is NOT expected to continue operating?
back:
Liquidation Value — the value of a business that is failing and expected to end or shut down. (pg. 296)

Memory Tip: Liquidation = Liquidate = Shut down.

front: What principle states that a buyer will not pay more for a property than the cost of buying another equally desirable property with the same utility?
back:
Principle of Substitution — mainly used in residential appraisals by comparing similar properties in the same market to determine market value. (pg. 297)

Memory Tip: Substitution = “Why pay more for the same thing?”

front: Which approach to value is typically used for a new property or a special-purpose property when there are no comparable properties available?
back:
Cost Depreciation Approach — commonly used for properties such as a courthouse, school, or church.

Memory Tip: Cost = New or Special

front: What do you call an improvement that is too excessive for the property or does not provide the best use of the investment?
back:
Over-Improvement — an improvement that is excessive compared with similar properties or does not make the best use of the property.

Example: Building a $100,000 luxury swimming pool in a neighborhood where similar homes have no pools and the added value does not justify the cost.

Memory Tip: Over = Too Much for the Property

front: What is the age a property appears to be based on its condition, updates, or wear and tear?
back:
Effective Age — the age the property appears to be, which may differ from its actual age due to extensive updates or excessive wear and tear. When estimating depreciation, the appraiser uses the effective age if both actual and effective age are given. (pg. 304)

Memory Tip: Effective = Looks Like

front: What is the basic operating statement formula used to calculate NOI (Net Operating Income)?
back:
PGI (Potential Gross Income)
− V&C (Vacancy & Collection Loss)
+ OI (Other Income)
= EGI (Effective Gross Income)
− OE (Operating Expenses)
= NOI (Net Operating Income)

Operating Expenses (OE): FE + VE + R
Fixed Expenses + Variable Expenses + Reserves

Memory Tip: Parents Visit Often Every Other Night
PGI → V&C → OI → EGI → OE → NOI

front: What comes after NOI when calculating an investment property's cash flow?
back:
NOI − ADS = BTCF (CTF)

NOI = Net Operating Income
ADS = Annual Debt Service (mortgage payments)
BTCF = Before-Tax Cash Flow

Then:
BTCF − Income Tax = ATCF

ATCF = After-Tax Cash Flow
Depreciation is a deduction used when calculating income tax.

Memory Tip: Night → By → Invitation → Alone
NOI → BTCF → ATCF

front: What is a disadvantage of real estate investing because property cannot be quickly converted into cash?
back:
Illiquidity — an asset that cannot be sold quickly for cash. Real estate is illiquid and immobile (local). (pg. 320)

Memory Tip: Illiquid = Not Easy to Turn Into Cash

front: What type of risk can be offset or protected against with insurance?
back:
Static Risk — risk that can be covered by insurance, such as fire, flood, and robbery.

Memory Tip: Static = Insurable

front: What is the value of a profitable business when the values of its real estate, personal property, and intangible assets are combined?
back:
Going Concern Value — the combined value of the business’s real estate + personal property + intangible assets, such as licenses, franchises, and noncompetition contracts.

Memory Tip: Going Concern = Everything Together

front: What does Florida’s Save Our Homes Act do for a homestead property?
back:
It limits annual increases in the property’s assessed value to 3% or the CPI, whichever is less. This applies to a primary residence (homestead). (pg. 346)

Example: When a buyer purchases a home, the property is reassessed, so the buyer may have a higher assessed value and higher property taxes than the previous owner.

Memory Tip: Save Our Homes = 3% or CPI, whichever is less.

front: Can a homeowner transfer the Save Our Homes benefit to a new homestead in Florida?
back:
Yes. The homeowner can transfer some or all of the Save Our Homes benefit to a new homestead anywhere in Florida.

If the new home is the same price or more expensive than the old home → the homeowner can transfer the actual cap savings.
Memory: Same or More = Transfer the Savings.

front: What is the maximum amount of Save Our Homes cap savings that can be transferred to a new homestead?
back:
$500,000 is the maximum amount of cap savings that can be transferred.

Memory: Transfer limit = $500K.

front: What is a Special Assessment Tax?
back:
A one-time tax levy used to pay for public improvements that add value to the property. (pg. 349)

Memory: Special = Specific improvement → One-time tax

front: What method calculates the cost of a public improvement based on the number of feet a property owner has along the street?
back:
Front Foot Basis — the cost is expressed per front-foot and allocated based on the property's street frontage. Used for street paving and sidewalk installation.

Memory: More frontage = More cost.

front: Why are developers in a PUD allowed to include smaller-than-normal lots, such as zero-lot-line lots and patio homes?
back:
To compensate developers for reserving land for common use in the PUD.

Memory: Common land = Smaller lots allowed.

⚠️ Exam Tip: Watch for EXCEPT / NOT Allowed questions.
